item.title: American Academy in Berlin: Berlin Prize Fellowship 2027-28
item.description:
Organisation: American Academy in Berlin

Location: Berlin, Germany, at the Hans Arnhold Center. RESTRICTED: fellowships are open only to citizens and permanent residents of the United States.

Award: Monthly stipend of USD 5,000, plus roundtrip airfare, accommodation at or near the Hans Arnhold Center, partial board, in-house library services and professional networking opportunities. Roughly two dozen fellowships awarded each year. No application fee.

Duration: One full academic semester (about 4 months). Fall runs mid-August to mid-December; spring runs late January to late May.

Deadline: 25 Sep 2026

The American Academy in Berlin is an independent, nonprofit institute for advanced study in the arts, humanities, social sciences, law, journalism and public policy, whose primary mission is to strengthen the cultural and intellectual ties between the United States and Germany. Each year, after a rigorous selection process, the Academy awards roughly two dozen semester-long Berlin Prize fellowships to individuals who demonstrate excellence in their fields. DISCIPLINES: applications are welcome across the humanities, social sciences, law, journalism and various areas of public policy. The Academy generally encourages projects addressing pressing issues of the day, specifically naming democracy, security, technology and society (especially AI), energy including climate, and global order. Dedicated fellowships also support projects in Jewish studies, German studies, and public health and biotechnology. Project proposals need not focus on Germany, but candidates should explain how a residency in Berlin would enhance their work. NOT ACCEPTED: proposals in mathematics or the natural sciences. NOTE FOR ARTISTS: visual artists and composers are invited through separate, nomination-based competitions, so there is no open application route for them here. ELIGIBILITY: fellowships are restricted to citizens and permanent residents of the United States. Both emerging and established figures are eligible. PhD holders qualify as emerging scholars with a strong record of peer-reviewed work beyond the dissertation; candidates in non-academic fields such as journalism, filmmaking and policy need a significant record of publication or production; fiction and nonfiction writers must have published at least one book with a reputable press. WHAT FELLOWS DO: fellows present their work to audiences in and around Berlin through lectures, readings, public discussions, performances and film screenings, and should be willing to engage with relevant German institutions, organizations and the media; these activities are integral to the Academy's mission of fostering transatlantic dialogue. APPLICATION MATERIALS: a project proposal of 1,500 to 1,750 words plus a one-page bibliography; a curriculum vitae of up to 10 pages; two writing samples totalling no more than 60 pages; and three letters of recommendation, which are due 2 October 2026. DEADLINE: Friday 25 September 2026 at 12:00 noon Eastern Time (18:00 Central European Time). TIMELINE: all candidates are notified of the competition outcome by email in late March 2027; the 2027-28 Berlin Prize recipients are announced in May 2027.

item.title: Science & Technology Policy Fellowships, 2027-28 Class
item.description:
Organisation: American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)

Location: Washington DC, USA. Fellows are placed in US federal executive, legislative and judicial branch offices and must reside in the DC area.

Award: Stipend depending on experience and placement, roughly USD 85,000 to 140,000; the dedicated AI legislative branch cohort is paid at GS-12 Step 10 on the DC locality scale. The AAAS Science & Technology Policy Fellowships place scientists and engineers inside US federal agencies, congressional offices and the judicial branch for a year of hands-on policymaking, contributing technical knowledge and analytical skills to the federal policy process. AI, data and computing policy placements are among the largest tracks, and AAAS runs a dedicated AI legislative branch cohort that places AI experts in congressional offices at GS-12 Step 10 on the DC locality scale. ELIGIBILITY: US citizens holding a PhD or equivalent doctoral degree in any science or engineering field, or a master's degree in engineering plus three years of post-degree professional experience; some tracks accept a bachelor's plus five years. Relevant expertise includes AI, machine learning, computer science, robotics and data science. Fellows must reside in DC, Maryland or northern Virginia during the fellowship year. TIMELINE: the application portal opens 1 August 2026 and closes 1 November 2026 at 11:59pm ET, with eligibility notification in late November, interview notification January to February 2027, semi-finalist interviews in March, placement offers by early May, and the fellowship year running 1 September 2027 to 31 August 2028. RESPONSIBILITIES: map segments of frontier AI and adjacent technology supply chains, with possible focus on specific country ecosystems or on actors across segments such as capital allocation, raw materials, mineral processing, chip design, fabrication, advanced packaging, datasets, datacentres and frontier labs; analyse how ownership stakes, trade relationships and control are likely to evolve under different technological, commercial and geopolitical scenarios; and develop strategic proposals for stakeholders across government and industry. item.title: Physical AI Safety Institute: Research Fellowship (expression of interest)
item.description:
Organisation: Physical AI Safety Institute (PAISI)

Location: Not stated in the call. PAISI is a US 501(c)(3) nonprofit and its team is affiliated with UC Berkeley and the Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago; because fellows are given access to physical robot platforms, expect an in-person or hybrid component. No nationality restriction is stated for expressions of interest.

Award: Stipend amount is not published. Fellows receive a stipend, access to physical robot platforms, compute for simulation and training, and structured mentorship. PAISI was seeded by a grant from BlueDot Impact. Free to submit an expression of interest.

Duration: 12 weeks per cohort. Target cohorts are Winter 2026, Spring 2027 and Summer 2027; the expression-of-interest form asks you to pick your preferred dates.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

Robot foundation models (pi-zero, OpenVLA, GR00T and others) are approaching widespread deployment on the back of more than USD 18 billion in funding, and almost nobody is working on their safety. The Physical AI Safety Institute, a new nonprofit founded by Bear Haon and Kaylene Stocking and seeded by a grant from BlueDot Impact, describes itself as a capacity-building organisation growing the community that develops techniques to interpret, align and control robot foundation models. Its research fellowship runs in 12-week cohorts: each fellow works within a stream led by a mentor on a concrete problem in physical AI safety, with mentors drawn from researchers with track records in robot foundation models, mechanistic interpretability, safe control or adversarial robustness for embodied systems. Each cohort ends with a research symposium where fellows present their work. STREAMS: mechanistic interpretability (sparse autoencoders and activation patching for VLA and WAM architectures); adversarial robustness (jailbreaking and prompt injection in the embodied action space); runtime monitoring (detecting when a policy operates outside its competence envelope); sim-to-real safety transfer (do safety behaviours survive deployment on physical hardware); and robot security (cyberattack vectors, data poisoning and supply chain for deployed robot models). WHO SHOULD APPLY: researchers with strong technical foundations in robotics or machine learning and a demonstrated interest in safety; prior safety experience is not required. PROCESS: this stage is an expression of interest, not a full application. The form takes about two minutes and asks you to pick your stream and preferred cohort dates; concrete details including stipend figures and application deadlines are shared through that channel, and neither is published on the site as of listing. PAISI also publishes seven free curriculum modules running from classical robot safety through VLA interpretability, adversarial robustness and runtime monitoring to deployment evaluation, plus a white paper, The Case for Physical AI Safety, at paisi.ai/the-case-for-physical-ai-safety. Contact: bear@paisi.ai.

item.title: Apollo Research: (Senior) AI Governance Researcher (London or San Francisco)
item.description:
Organisation: Apollo Research

Location: In-person in Apollo's London or San Francisco office, with flexible hours and work-from-home arrangements. Visa sponsorship available in the UK and the US, not guaranteed for every candidate.

Award: USD 150,000 to 225,000 salary plus equity. Benefits include unlimited vacation and sick leave, up to 6 months paid parental leave, health/dental/vision insurance, employer-matched retirement savings, meals on workdays, paid work trips and retreats, and a USD 1,000 yearly professional development budget. Note: a widely circulated newsletter listing quoted this range in pounds; the posting itself says USD.

Duration: Full-time, permanent

Deadline: Rolling / undated

A mid to senior research role on the Governance team at Apollo Research, a startup working on the threats from scheming frontier AI systems that works with and is trusted by every frontier AI lab, doing fundamental research, pre-deployment model testing and scheming mitigations. THE TEAM: Governance researches the institutional, legal and strategic implications of AI scheming and loss-of-control threats, working alongside the Science of Scheming, Evaluations and Monitoring teams. Its stated bet is that the governance, risk-management and legal frameworks built inside and outside frontier labs over the next two years will help determine collective ability to stay in control of increasingly advanced systems. Focus areas: scheming, loss of control, governance of models deployed internally by frontier labs, government testing of frontier AI for high-stakes use, and the handoff of AI R&D to AIs. TRACK RECORD: the loss-of-control chapter of the International AI Safety Report 2026; the report 'AI Behind Closed Doors: A Primer on the Governance of Internal Deployment'; 'The Loss of Control Playbook: Degrees, Dynamics, and Preparedness'; a TIME op-ed with Yoshua Bengio; peer-reviewed work on precursory capabilities, AI incident regimes and National Security Benchmarks for Loss of Control presented at ICML, IASEAI and the UK AI Security Institute's Conference on Frontier AI Safety Frameworks. The team briefs governments on both sides of the Atlantic, including Congressional committees and the intelligence community; some work is non-public. THE WORK: design and drive AI governance research on critical safety and security questions; lead research across formats including peer-reviewed papers, in-depth reports, technical memos and legal analyses; scope forward-looking projects grounded in the technical state of the art; engage with legal, policy and governance frameworks alongside partners in companies and governments; and translate technical AI safety literature and colleagues' empirical work into governance-relevant proposals. REQUIREMENTS: a minimum of 6 years work experience from academia, industry and/or private practice, and a track record of substantive research outputs that shifted thinking in the field (peer-reviewed publications, high-impact reports, a relevant PhD thesis or comparable). Apollo says it will assess fit on individual merit and can tailor scope and title for the right person. APPLICATION: resume plus relevant work samples or links; a cover letter is optional but welcome, especially if it sketches the research direction you would pursue. DEADLINE: none. Reviewed on a ROLLING basis, and Apollo says it aims to finalise a hire as soon as possible, so apply early.

item.title: CSET (Georgetown): Frontier AI Research Lead (Research Fellow or Senior Fellow)
item.description:
Organisation: Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), Georgetown University Walsh School of Foreign Service

Location: Washington DC, US. Based in the United States, no relocation assistance. NO VISA SPONSORSHIP: applicants must be legally eligible to work in the US without sponsorship from Georgetown University.

Award: Research Fellow: roughly USD 100,000 to 130,000 per year. Senior Fellow: roughly USD 160,000 to 190,000 per year. Commensurate with experience. Georgetown University benefits. No application fee.

Duration: Full-time, permanent

Deadline: Rolling / undated

CSET, the policy research organisation inside Georgetown's Walsh School of Foreign Service, is hiring someone to lead a new Frontier AI team, at either Research Fellow or Senior Fellow level depending on experience. THE RESEARCH: expanding CSET's work on cutting-edge general-purpose AI, building on the CyberAI Project and the Foundational Research Grants program, to give policymakers clarity about current capabilities, use cases and risks; where the frontier moves next, including the prospects for AGI or superintelligence and what would alter them; and how new evidence should change expectations. Named priority areas: Chinese frontier AI efforts, the development and deployment of increasingly capable AI agents, making sense of conflicting evidence about capabilities and risks, and assessing the compute demands of frontier systems. Understanding why experts disagree, and what that means for policy, is a recurring theme. THE ROLE: shape priorities and overall research strategy, oversee execution and report production, and help hire and manage supporting researchers including Research Analysts and Student Research Assistants. Fellows also brief policymakers, speak at public events, act as subject-matter experts for media, and work with CSET's data team on empirical analyses. Reports to CSET's Director of Analysis. WHO THEY WANT: comfort interpreting technical AI/ML research (large language models, multimodal systems, reinforcement learning) and distilling it into policy-relevant insight, plus comfort with empirical data and qualitative methods such as in-depth interviews. Deep familiarity with the frontier AI landscape and expertise in at least one of: safety, security and governance debates including dangerous capabilities, loss-of-control risks and systemic effects; applied experience developing, training, deploying or evaluating large-scale models; compute requirements, scaling laws and infrastructure; or Chinese AI research, policy and deployment. REQUIRED OF ALL CANDIDATES: a graduate degree (Master's, JD or PhD) in a relevant field, ability to research, write, brief and manage with limited supervision, familiarity with interpreting and visualising data, and project or team management experience. Research Fellow level needs at least 3 years in research and policy analysis; Senior Fellow needs at least 5 years of public service in senior roles or 10 years of progressive private-sector roles, plus demonstrated mentoring experience. DEADLINE: none published; applications are reviewed on a rolling basis.

item.title: Good Life Residents Program: AI and Finance
item.description:
Organisation: Roosevelt Institute, in partnership with Data & Society

Location: Remote. Travel may be requested for select convenings and for the culminating public event. US economic policy focus.

Award: USD 3,000 stipend, plus travel and accommodation for the culminating event if needed. No application fee.

Duration: 6 months, part-time at roughly 5 to 8 hours per month

Deadline: Rolling / undated

The Good Life Residents Program is a six-month Roosevelt Institute initiative that develops new leaders and elevates bold ideas across six economic policy priorities under its Good Life Agenda. Each topic area hosts a cohort of 3 to 4 residents plus 1 to 2 senior Topic Advisors (academics, policy leaders, organizers or government practitioners) who provide strategic and intellectual mentorship and moderate the closing event. Residents write a roughly 1,500-word original policy essay advancing a people-centered policy vision against a topic-specific prompt, take part in structured dialogue with peers, Topic Advisors and Roosevelt Think Tank directors, help prepare and appear at a culminating public event, contribute to press opportunities such as op-eds and reporter calls where applicable, and act as ambassadors for the Good Life Agenda in their professional and public networks. The current round, the AI and Finance Residents Program, is run in partnership with Data & Society and asks for bold ideas on how to shape, redirect, interrupt or make more visible and contestable the flows of capital into generative AI. Framing: breakneck investment in generative AI technology and infrastructure is distorting the stock market, profit measures, bond issuance, the pace and composition of growth, job creation and trade policy, with seven tech companies accounting for more than a third of S&P 500 market capitalisation and complex, sometimes circular financial arrangements obscuring risk. Suggested lines of inquiry include what government interventions could improve public oversight, risk allocation and direction-setting in private markets; how other investments could be coordinated and scaled if AI spending is crowding them out; what role public spending or new institutions could play in catalysing technology R&D designed to support workers, sustainability and supply chains; what democratic input mechanisms would keep state influence over capital flows less vulnerable to corruption; and how federal AI policy should address public hostility to data centre investments alongside national security and competitiveness. Compensation is USD 3,000 plus travel and accommodation for the culminating event. FLAG: Roosevelt does not publish an application deadline for the AI and Finance round on the programme page, and earlier rounds (Social Security financing, Federal Reserve powers, housing) each ran their own short application window. Check the Formstack application form linked from the programme page for the current closing date before applying.

item.description:

Duration: 18-month full-time fellowship (2026-27)

The Institute for Advanced Study is seeking a 2026-27 Civic Science Fellow to advance understanding of the social, democratic and scientific implications of artificial intelligence. The full-time, 18-month position is based in the Science, Technology, and Social Values Lab led by Harold F. Linder Professor of Social Science Alondra Nelson. Working closely with Professor Nelson and Lab members, the Fellow contributes to research and policy analysis and to scholarly and public-facing publications, and supports multidisciplinary, multisector initiatives at the intersection of AI, science and governance. DUTIES (75% Lab work): conduct original research on the Lab's AI-and-society agenda; synthesize scholarship on the social implications of AI, sociotechnical approaches to AI governance and the epistemological implications of AI in research; contribute policy research on governance mechanisms that strengthen democratic institutions; help organize convenings and working groups; collaborate on manuscripts, reports and grant proposals; support editorial development of publications; and develop public-facing essays, policy briefs and digital materials. The remaining 25% supports the Fellow's own independent research, network-building and full participation in the intellectual life of IAS. MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS: a PhD in the social sciences, sciences or humanities; a strong record of scholarly research, writing and publication on the social implications of science and technology or related fields; and exceptional writing and editing skills for both academic and non-academic audiences. Preferred: specialization in science and technology studies, science and technology policy, organizational studies or qualitative methods, and demonstrated engagement with AI governance and technology policy debates. Apply with a cover letter and resume via the IAS/Paylocity posting.

item.title: CHAI: Research Fellowship (Center for Human-Compatible AI, UC Berkeley)
item.description:
Organisation: Center for Human-Compatible AI (CHAI), UC Berkeley

Location: Berkeley, California, USA (in-person)

Award: Salary commensurate with qualifications and experience, on UC Berkeley salary scales (negotiated). Funding for two years, renewable up to three given satisfactory performance. Eligible for visa sponsorship, with CHAI also contributing to visa costs for fellows and their dependents. No application fee.

Duration: Two years, renewable up to three

Deadline: Rolling / undated

The CHAI Research Fellowship trains highly qualified postdoctoral researchers to advance beneficial AI, working with CHAI faculty Stuart Russell, Pieter Abbeel and Anca Dragan and collaborating with affiliate faculty at Berkeley AI Research and beyond. Fellows have broad freedom to pursue novel research toward provably beneficial AI systems in areas such as reasoning, decision making, learning, multi-agent systems and philosophical foundations, using probability theory, game theory and control theory. Current topics of interest include theoretical foundations of intelligent agent architecture, expressive formal languages for probability models (including probabilistic programming), decision making over long time scales, cumulative lifelong learning, human-in-the-loop planning and reinforcement learning, human-robot interaction, the structure of human preferences, acting on behalf of multiple humans, robust cooperation in heterogeneous multi-agent systems, and mechanism design for human-machine systems. Fellows may also lead collaborations, advise junior researchers, and teach. QUALIFICATIONS: a PhD (or about to be obtained) in a relevant technical discipline (computer science, statistics, mathematics, or theoretical economics) and a record of high-quality published research; prior work on the AI control problem is not required. International applicants are eligible (visa sponsorship provided). TO APPLY: submit via the CHAI application form a resume, a one-page statement of interest describing the research you would like to undertake, and the names and emails of two academic referees. Start date is flexible and applications are reviewed on a rolling basis (no fixed deadline). General enquiries: chai-info@berkeley.edu.

item.title: Human Rights Watch: AI Strategy and Solutions Lead (one-year fixed term)
item.description:
Organisation: Human Rights Watch (HRW), Operations Department

Location: Must be within commuting distance of an HRW office: Amsterdam, Amman, Berlin, Brussels, London, Stockholm, New York, Washington DC, Miami, Sao Paulo, Toronto or Chicago. Reports to the Chief Information Officer in Berlin. No relocation support and no work-authorisation sponsorship.

Award: USD 102,000 to 112,000 plus employer-paid benefits if based in the US; ranges outside the US are set by local market conditions. No application fee.

Duration: One year fixed-term, full time. Application deadline 30 August 2026.

Deadline: Closed 30 Aug 2026

Human Rights Watch is hiring an AI Strategy and Solutions Lead into its Operations Department to build the foundation for responsible AI adoption across the organisation. The role deliberately sits between strategy and execution: assessing organisational readiness, mapping partnerships and governance, and also prototyping and shipping working systems. THE WORK, in four strands. (1) STRATEGY AND READINESS: with the CIO and the Information Security and Technology (IST) leadership team, build an AI strategy covering data foundation requirements, infrastructure gaps and organisational readiness; assess current state and shape a roadmap balancing quick wins against long-term capacity; research what peer nonprofit, humanitarian and human rights organisations are doing and find collaboration openings. (2) FLAGSHIP SOLUTIONS: work with departments to find high-impact use cases, translate business needs into technical approaches, build and deploy AI/ML solutions with measurable value (time saved, efficiency, better outcomes), using the Microsoft AI ecosystem (Copilot Studio, Azure AI, Power Platform) among other tools, and oversee consultants and vendors to extend delivery capacity. (3) ADOPTION AND CAPACITY: balance onboarding staff onto AI tools against building custom solutions where they amplify the organisation's strengths; write training material pitched at different work areas and skill levels covering prompting and responsible use; support working groups and communities of practice; produce playbooks and guides for non-technical staff.
